lessons.title: Branching basics
objectives: Create and switch branches, and understand HEAD
Explain how branch changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect branch with git checkout -b and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A branch is an independent line of development -- you can experiment on a branch without affecting others. git checkout -b feature creates a new branch called feature and switches to it immediately.
examples:
git checkout -b feature
# now on branch 'feature', HEAD points here
git branch          # lists all local branches
commonMistakes: Forgetting which branch you're currently on before making changes -- always check with `git status` or `git branch`, which marks the current branch.
lessons.careerRelevance: Branching is what makes safe, parallel experimentation possible on real projects.

lessons.title: Merging & conflicts
objectives: Merge branches and resolve a merge conflict
Explain how merge changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect merge with merge conflict and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: git merge combines changes from one branch into another. A merge conflict happens when Git can't automatically reconcile changes to the same lines and needs manual resolution -- you edit the conflicting file, choose the correct content, then commit.
examples:
git checkout main
git merge feature
# if there's a conflict, Git marks the file --
# edit it, then:
git add resolved_file.txt
git commit
commonMistakes: Panicking and discarding all changes when a merge conflict appears -- conflicts are a normal, expected part of merging and are meant to be resolved, not avoided.
lessons.careerRelevance: Merging and resolving conflicts confidently is a core, daily collaborative-development skill.

lessons.title: Working with remotes
objectives: Clone, push, and pull from a remote repository
Explain how remote changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect remote with origin and predict what changes when one assumption changes

lessons.explanation: A remote is a reference to a version of the repository hosted elsewhere (like GitHub) -- origin is the conventional name for the main one. git clone <url> downloads a full copy including history.
examples:
git clone https://github.com/user/repo.git
git push origin main
git pull origin main
commonMistakes: Running git push without first git pull-ing recent changes -- this can be rejected if the remote has commits you don't have locally yet.
lessons.careerRelevance: Working with remotes is how real collaborative work actually gets shared and synced.

lessons.title: Undoing changes: revert, reset & stash
objectives: Safely undo a commit, and temporarily shelve changes
Explain how git revert changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect git revert with git reset and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: git revert <commit> creates a NEW commit that undoes a previous one -- safe for shared history since nothing is deleted. git reset rewrites history instead, which is risky if that history has already been pushed and shared.
examples:
git revert a1b2c3d      # safe: adds an undo commit
git stash                # shelve current uncommitted changes
git stash pop            # restore them later
commonMistakes: Using git reset on commits that have already been pushed and shared -- this rewrites history other people's copies still expect, causing confusion.
lessons.careerRelevance: Knowing when to revert vs reset vs stash prevents real, sometimes hard-to-recover mistakes.
lessons.explain: git revert <commit> creates a NEW commit that undoes a previous one -- safe for shared history since nothing is deleted. git reset rewrites history instead, which is risky if that history has already been pushed and shared.

lessons.title: Inspecting history: log, diff & commit hashes
objectives: Read commit history and see what changed
Explain how git log changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect git log with git log --oneline and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: git log shows the commit history: hashes, authors, dates, and messages. git log --oneline condenses this to one line per commit.
examples:
git log --oneline
git diff              # what's changed but not yet staged
git diff --staged     # what's staged but not yet committed
commonMistakes: Only ever looking at the latest commit and never checking `git log`/`git diff` when investigating when or why something changed.
lessons.careerRelevance: Reading history fluently is essential for debugging 'this used to work' problems.

lessons.title: Ignoring files & commit hygiene
objectives: Use .gitignore and write commits that are easy to review later
Explain how .gitignore changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect .gitignore with commit messages and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: .gitignore lists files and patterns Git should never track (build artifacts, secrets, local config) -- keeping the repository clean. Small, focused commits with clear messages are easier to review, understand later, and revert individually if something goes wrong, compared to one giant commit covering unrelated changes.
examples:
.gitignore contents:
node_modules/
*.log
.env

# good commit message: 'Fix null pointer in checkout flow'
# not: 'stuff' or 'fix'
commonMistakes: Committing generated files (build output, dependencies) directly into the repository instead of ignoring them -- this bloats the repo and causes unnecessary merge conflicts.
lessons.careerRelevance: Clean commit hygiene is one of the most visible signals of an experienced collaborator.

lessons.title: Collaborating with pull requests
objectives: Understand what a pull request is for
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: branch protection rules, required CI checks.
Explain how pull request changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect pull request with branch protection rules and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A pull request (or merge request) is a proposal to merge changes from one branch into another, typically reviewed by teammates before merging -- it's the standard way real teams review and discuss code changes before they become part of the main branch.
examples:
# typical flow:
# 1. git checkout -b my-feature
# 2. make changes, commit, git push origin my-feature
# 3. open a pull request on GitHub comparing my-feature -> main
# 4. teammates review, discuss, request changes if needed
# 5. merge once approved
commonMistakes: Pushing directly to a shared main branch without review, on a team that expects pull requests -- this skips the review step meant to catch issues before they land.
lessons.careerRelevance: Pull requests are the standard collaboration workflow at almost every real software company. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Rebasing & Rewriting History
objectives: Use rebase to keep a clean, linear history, and know when rebasing a branch is genuinely unsafe
Explain how rebase changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect rebase with interactive rebase and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Merging preserves exactly what happened, including a merge commit tying two branches together; rebasing replays your branch's commits on top of another branch's latest state instead, producing a clean, linear history with no merge commit.
examples:
# clean up your OWN unpushed commits before opening a PR:
git rebase -i HEAD~3
# lets you squash 'wip', 'fix typo', 'actually fix it' into one clean commit

# update your feature branch on top of main's latest commits:
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main

# NEVER do this on a branch others have already pulled:
git push --force   # rewrites history that others may depend on -- breaks their repo
commonMistakes: Rebasing (and force-pushing) a branch that's already been pushed and pulled by teammates -- this rewrites history they've already built work on top of, and force-pushing then makes their.
lessons.careerRelevance: Interactive rebase for clean commit history before a PR, combined with knowing exactly when NOT to rebase, is a routine expectation on any team working with Git collaboratively.
lessons.explain: Merging preserves exactly what happened, including a merge commit tying two branches together; rebasing replays your branch's commits on top of another branch's latest state instead, producing a clean, linear history with no merge commit.

description: Version control — the habit every engineer needs from day one.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the practical difference between merge and rebase, and when would you choose each?
interviewPreparation.a: Merge preserves exactly what happened, including a merge commit joining two branches -- honest history, but can get tangled with many contributors. Rebase replays your commits on top of the target branch, producing clean linear history, but rewrites commit hashes -- fine for your own not-yet-shared work, unsafe for branches others have already pulled.

interviewPreparation.q: Why is it dangerous to rebase and force-push a branch that others have already pulled?
interviewPreparation.a: Rebasing rewrites commit history -- the commits get new hashes. If someone else already pulled the old commits and built work on top of them, force-pushing the rebased branch effectively erases the history their work depends on, leaving them with confusing conflicts and duplicate-looking commits when they try to reconcile.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you clean up a messy sequence of commits (like several 'wip' commits) before opening a pull request?
interviewPreparation.a: Interactive rebase (`git rebase -i`) against your own not-yet-shared commits, squashing the messy intermediate commits into one or a few clean, well-described commits -- since these commits haven't been pushed/shared yet, rewriting them is completely safe.

interviewPreparation.q: How do you resolve a merge conflict in a shared file?
interviewPreparation.a: Open the conflicted file, look at the conflict markers showing both versions, decide (often with the other author) what the correct combined result should be, remove the markers, stage the resolved file, and complete the merge with a commit -- ideally with a message explaining the resolution, not just 'fix conflict.'

interviewPreparation.q: What makes a pull request description actually useful to a reviewer?
interviewPreparation.a: What changed and why, not just what -- the reasoning a reviewer would otherwise have to reconstruct by reading every diff line by line. A good description lets a reviewer approach the code with the right context before they've read a single line of it.

careerApplications: Expected baseline on any engineering team from day one.

capstone.title: Manage a realistic collaborative Git workflow, cleanly and safely
capstone.description: Simulate a real team workflow on a repository: feature branches, a clean commit history achieved through interactive rebase (not just merge commits everywhere), a genuinely resolved merge conflict, and a pull request with a clear description. This capstone is about Git discipline under realistic collaborative conditions, not just knowing individual commands in isolation.
deliverables: A repository with a clean, readable commit history -- meaningful commit messages, no 'wip' or 'fix typo' commits left in via interactive rebase before merging
At least one feature branch rebased onto the latest main before merging, keeping history linear
A genuinely resolved merge conflict (not avoided) with a commit message explaining the resolution
A pull request with a clear description of what changed and why, as if a real reviewer needed to understand it without asking you
A written note on one situation where you would use merge instead of rebase, and why
capstone.portfolioTips: A repo with genuinely clean history and a well-written PR description is a small, quick thing for a reviewer to check -- and one of the fastest ways to signal you'd be easy to collaborate with on a real team, versus someone who's only used Git solo.

industryUsage.usage: Built its entire product around the pull-request collaboration workflow this capstone practices -- clear PR descriptions and clean history are exactly what makes code review efficient at any company using it.
Has historically favored a clean, linear commit history (often enforced via tooling) over a tangled merge-commit graph, treating commit hygiene as a real code-review criterion, not just a preference.
The project Git itself was built for -- famously strict about clean, well-described, logically separated commits, and a widely cited example of why commit hygiene matters at scale.
